title: Product owner, team coach, developer and tester
blurb: Explain the four delivery team roles and match a person's background to the role that fits them best.
question: A team member designs and runs checks that each product meets its acceptance criteria and the team's Definition of Done. Which PRINCE2 Agile role is this?

teach.body: Each delivery team has the same make-up: a product owner (PO) who leads it, a team coach who helps it work well, and developers and testers who create and check the products. The team self-manages how it does the work, within tolerances agreed with the project manager. With several teams, each has its own product owner, and a team coach may serve one or two teams.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Figure 7.1, Figure 7.2, Table 7.2

head: Role
In one line
Typical task
rows: Owns and maintains the product backlog
Reviews products against the team DoD
teach.caption: Paraphrased from Table 7.2 and Table B.1.

teach.h: Product owner: a version of the team manager
teach.body: The PO delivers the work allocated to the team within the tolerances and constraints agreed with the project manager, and agrees work package descriptions with the PM. They own the product backlog, prepare and maintain it and its user stories, and keep it aligned with the project backlog, continued business justification and project tolerances. They act as a servant leader and work closely with the chief product owner.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2, Table B.1

teach.h: Team coach: inside one or two teams
teach.body: The team coach works closely with one or two specific teams to improve their effectiveness. They help the teams self-manage, build trust and accountability, refine processes, resolve conflicts and improve communication. They balance self-management with PRINCE2 Agile principles and tolerances, help write user stories, facilitate team workshops and coach agile best practices. A Scrum master fits this role.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2, Table B.1

teach.body: Developers design, develop and maintain increments of products, contribute to their design, resolve technical issues and keep improving the outputs. Testers make sure products are of good quality and reliable by designing, running and possibly automating tests or quality reviews. They build quality assurance into each iteration and review products against acceptance or quality criteria and the team Definition of Done.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 7.2, Table B.1

teach.h: Which delivery role fits this person?
Scrum names and PRINCE2 Agile roles
head: Scrum accountability
Closest PRINCE2 Agile role
teach.caption: A teaching aid. The book states that a Scrum master fits the team coach role.

teach.body: Ashgrove Veterinary Group is building an appointment app. Practice operations lead Fiona Rees becomes product owner: she owns the team's product backlog and agrees sets of user stories with the project manager. Callum Ng, who has run agile teams before, is team coach and facilitates the team planning workshop. Two app builders are developers, and data analyst Priya Desai, who measures booking success, becomes the tester.

teach.text: The product owner owns ONE team's product backlog and does not prioritize across teams (that is the CPO). The team coach supports the team but has no authority over it; the PO holds that line. Someone who measures or checks results fits TESTER, not developer.

items: PO: version of the team manager; delivers within tolerances agreed with the PM.
PO owns the product backlog and aligns it with the project backlog.
Team coach: one or two teams; self-management, workshops, user stories, best practice.
A Scrum master fits the team coach role.
Developer: designs, builds and maintains increments of products.
Tester: designs and runs tests; checks against acceptance criteria and the team DoD.

summary: You can now explain the responsibilities of the product owner, team coach, developer and tester. You can also match a person's background to the delivery role that suits them.

A.q: Which role owns a delivery team's product backlog?
A.why: The product owner owns the product backlog and keeps it aligned with the project backlog (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: The team coach helps the team self-manage and write user stories but does not own the backlog.
whyNot.1: The CPO owns the project backlog, not each team's product backlog.
whyNot.3: The PM consults POs on product backlogs but does not own them.

A.q: How many teams does a team coach typically work closely with?
options: Up to six teams at once
A.why: The team coach works closely with one or two specific teams (Table 7.2).

whyNot.1: Working across the organization describes the agile coach.
whyNot.2: Six teams is far beyond the stated scope; a team coach works closely with one or two teams.
whyNot.3: Team coach assignment is by team, not by management stage.

A.q: Which role designs, develops and maintains increments of products?
A.why: Developers design, develop and maintain increments of products during the project (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: Testers design and run tests and review products against the DoD.
whyNot.1: The team coach supports the team's ways of working rather than building products.
whyNot.2: The PO leads delivery and owns the backlog rather than building increments.

B.q: A candidate has worked as a Scrum master, helping teams to try out agile ways of working. Which PRINCE2 Agile role suits them BEST?
B.why: A Scrum master fits the team coach role, which guides one or two teams in adopting agile best practices (Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: The agile coach works at organization level on systemic blockers, beyond a single team.
whyNot.2: The PO leads delivery and owns the backlog; a Scrum master's experience is coaching.
whyNot.3: Project support provides administrative help, not team coaching.

B.q: An analyst whose job is to measure the impact of each release against agreed criteria joins a delivery team. Which role fits them BEST?
B.why: Testers make sure products meet the defined quality and acceptance criteria, so an analyst who measures impact fits tester (Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: Developers design and build outputs; measuring against criteria is testing work.
whyNot.1: The team coach helps the team self-manage rather than measuring results.
whyNot.3: The PO owns the backlog and leads delivery rather than checking against criteria.

B.q:
Which two statements about the product owner are correct?
1. The PO agrees work package descriptions with the project manager.
2. The PO sets priorities across all delivery teams.
3. The PO works closely with the chief product owner.
4. The PO approves tolerances for agile decision-making.
B.why: The PO agrees work package descriptions with the PM (1) and works closely with the CPO (3) (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: priorities across teams are set by the CPO.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: the CPO prioritizes across teams, and the executive approves agile tolerances.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is wrong: approving agile tolerances is the project executive's job.

C.q: Who facilitates team workshops, and who reviews products against the team Definition of Done?
C.why: The team coach facilitates team workshops, and the tester reviews products against acceptance criteria and the team DoD (Table B.1).

whyNot.1: The PO owns the backlog, and developers build rather than review against the DoD.
whyNot.2: The agile coach works at organization level, and assurance checks governance, not each product.
whyNot.3: The PM runs the project, and the team coach does not review products against the DoD.

C.q: Which role is the only one with a direct line of authority over developers and testers, and which role directs it?
C.why: The PO is the only role with direct authority over delivery team members, and the PM is the only role with direct authority over the PO (Figure 7.1).

whyNot.0: The team coach supports but does not direct the team, and the agile coach works across the organization.
whyNot.1: The CPO prioritizes across teams but does not directly manage team members.
whyNot.3: The PM directs the PO, not the individual developers and testers.

C.q: Which statement BEST describes how the team coach balances agile and PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Sets the team's time and cost tolerances each iteration
Guides teams to self-manage within principles and tolerances
Decides which user stories the team will deliver
Reports team status directly to the project board
C.why: The team coach guides teams in balancing agile self-management with PRINCE2 Agile principles and tolerances (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: Tolerances are set from above; time and cost have zero tolerance by default.
whyNot.2: Story selection is a team decision in iteration planning, led through the PO's backlog.
whyNot.3: Team progress goes to the PM through the team dashboard, not directly to the board.

reteach.title: A restaurant kitchen
reteach.question: In a busy kitchen, who decides the menu for this kitchen, who coaches the brigade, who cooks and who checks every plate before it leaves?

blocks.body: The head chef who owns this kitchen's menu and agrees orders with the restaurant manager is the product owner. The kitchen coach who helps the brigade work together is the team coach. The cooks are developers. The person who checks each plate against the standard before it goes out is the tester.

blocks.text: The head chef runs ONE kitchen's menu. Choosing priorities across a chain of kitchens is the CPO's job.

explain.body: A version of the team manager. Owns the product backlog, agrees work packages with the PM and delivers within agreed tolerances.

test.q: Within whose agreed tolerances and constraints does the product owner deliver the team's work?
test.why: POs deliver the work allocated to them within the tolerances and constraints agreed with the project manager (Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: The CPO sets priorities across teams but does not agree work package tolerances with the PO.
whyNot.1: The team coach supports the team and has no authority to set tolerances.
whyNot.2: The senior supplier represents the supplier side at governance level.

explain.body: Works with one or two teams: self-management, trust, conflict resolution, communication, user stories, workshops and continual improvement.

test.q: Which is a responsibility of the team coach?
options: Assisting the team with writing user stories
test.why: The team coach assists the delivery team with writing user stories (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: The product owner owns the product backlog.
whyNot.2: Work package descriptions are agreed between the PM and the PO.
whyNot.3: Removing systemic blockers across the organization is the agile coach's role.

explain.body: Designs, develops and maintains increments of products, resolves technical issues and continually improves the outputs.

test.q: A content designer who will write and produce an app's help pages joins a team. Which role fits them BEST?
test.why: Developers design, build and maintain outputs, so someone producing the content fits the developer role (Table 7.2).

whyNot.1: Testers check outputs against criteria rather than producing them.
whyNot.2: The team coach helps the team work well rather than creating content.
whyNot.3: Project support provides administrative help to the project, not product creation.

explain.body: Designs, runs and possibly automates tests or quality reviews, builds quality assurance into iterations and reviews products against acceptance criteria and the team DoD.

test.q: Against what does the tester review products?
options: Acceptance criteria and the team DoD
The delegation matrix and skill matrix
test.why: Testers review products against acceptance or quality criteria and the team Definition of Done (Table B.1).

whyNot.0: The project canvas is the business justification, reviewed by the board and assurance.
whyNot.1: The release map is the plan; it is not the standard a product is tested against.
whyNot.3: The delegation and skill matrices concern decisions and skills, not product quality.
